sections.html:
• Common names: Cuban crayfish, Blue Cuban crayfish
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Keeping: Easy; breeding: Easy–Medium
  • Optimal GH: 3–25; KH: 3–20
  • Diet: detritivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: aggressive as adults, very aggressive as juveniles
  • Colour forms: blue (dark to light blue) and brown

Cuban crayfish are endemic to Cuba, where they occur in scattered localities except in the southwestern mountains. According to studies, this species has a very restricted range of approximately 15,000 km2.

So far, there are no reports of Cuban crayfish in natural habitats outside their native range.
Cuban crayfish occupy a range of freshwater environments including slow streams, rivers, ponds, and swamps.

The minimum recommended tank size for one Cuban crayfish is 40 litres. A pair (male and female) requires at least 60 litres. If you are going to breed them, consider a separate tank for the offspring.

Crayfish can climb vertical surfaces and often use this ability to escape, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Temperature: lives well at room temperature, 18–22 °C, but easily tolerates a wide range of 15–33 °C.

pH: ideally 7.0–8.5.

Hardness: KH 3–20 and GH 3–25.

Dissolved oxygen: in laboratory experiments, even when the water in their tanks was changed only once every 2–3 weeks, the animals never showed signs of oxygen deficit.

This is a very hardy species; some scientists have used them as model organisms for over 20 years because of their low requirements for external conditions (Burmistrov and Shuranova, 1996). They are insensitive to water quality.

Filtration: only two real options, hang-on-back or canister filters. Sponge filters are a very bad idea, as the crayfish will chip, chew and break them apart.

Lighting: Cuban crayfish are nocturnal and prefer subdued lighting; basically any lighting will do.

Substrate: small gravel and/or sand is ideal.

Decorations: shelter and protection from predators is a key requirement. They like spots as narrow as they can fit in. They appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, wood, PVC pipes and other decorations. Give them a lot of hiding places, at least 2 per crayfish. This is especially vital for breeding or keeping them in a community tank, and is crucial for molting, as cannibalism after molting can become a big problem.

Acclimation: despite their hardiness, do not forget to acclimate them.

Cuban crayfish are opportunistic omnivores, eating both animal and plant material, dead or alive. They have a strong preference for high protein supplemented with a variety of vegetables and cereals: 20–30% of the diet for adults and 30–40% for juveniles. Adults can be more herbivorous, whereas juveniles tend to be more predatory, relying on protein for rapid growth.

Suitable foods:

  • Shrimp food (pellets, granules, flakes)
  • Fish food
  • Blanched vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrots, cucumbers, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.)
  • Fruits (apple, banana, pear, melon, mango, etc.)
  • Leaves
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Detritus worms
  • Brine shrimp
  • Tubifex worms
  • Blackworms
  • Earthworms
  • Freshly crushed snails
  • Dead fish or shrimp, etc.

Leaves (such as Indian almond leaves, dead beech or oak leaves) should always be on the menu. Make sure they get enough calcium for the exoskeleton by regularly feeding specialized invert foods with eggshells, cuttlebone, etc.

Adults can be fed 2–3 times a week, whereas juveniles should be fed daily. Cuban crayfish are aggressive, so do not let them starve or they will go after fish, fry, snails, shrimp, or even cannibalize.

Crayfish are slow eaters; leave food for 24 hours before removing it. Leaves can stay for several days. Remove whatever is not consumed in a day to prevent water contamination. Crayfish often store food in their hiding spots, so check them from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination. Change the diet regularly. It is better to feed at night, or at least in the evening, to replicate natural feeding conditions.

Procambarus cubensis is an aggressive and territorial species. Like most crayfish, they are natural loners, not social, and do not like to be kept in groups. They readily display aggressive postures towards anything around them and will almost certainly fight almost anybody of their size. Juveniles are also very aggressive and compete strongly for resources; according to some reports, cannibalism is one of the main ways their numbers are regulated.

Although fully aquatic, these crayfish are excellent climbers and will try to get out of any tank.

They are nocturnal, with extremely low activity during the day, becoming active almost exclusively at twilight and in darkness. Although they have a highly developed visual system, they do not rely on their eyes to orient, but use their antennae to explore a new environment.

They are natural diggers, often at the edge of water bodies. In aquariums, if there are not enough hiding places, they can push out some substrate to make their own dens. They are messy and destructive and will redecorate your aquascape to their liking.

  • Social: No
  • Active: No
  • Peaceful: No
  • Burrowers: Yes

Ideally, have a separate rearing tank.

Maturity: depending on temperature, Cuban crayfish reach sexual maturity at 6–8 months old. They can breed all year round.

Mating: the males initiate the process and use their claws to grasp and hold the female during copulation, which can last up to a few hours. After fertilization, females retreat to shelter and incubate the eggs, rarely coming out even to feed. Throw some food very close to her so she does not have to come out.

Eggs: the number varies with female size and water temperature. In warm conditions, large females can carry a few hundred eggs; low temperatures reduce fecundity to a few dozen. Females use their appendages to keep the eggs clean and well oxygenated. Egg mortality is high: out of a few hundred eggs, only 50–70 make it to hatchlings.

Hatching: eggs hatch within 4–6 weeks. There are no larval stages; all development occurs inside the egg, so a tiny copy of the adult emerges. Newly hatched young cannot live separately from the mother and stay with her for almost 2 weeks, after which they leave as completely independent miniature adults.

Generally, brooding females do not cannibalize eggs and young, but juveniles do. Frequent molting and competition for resources leading to a size hierarchy only aggravate the situation. Juveniles can be fed the same food as adults, in smaller portions.

Cuban crayfish do not grow very large. On average, this species grows only to 5–7 cm long. Males usually grow larger than females. Some individuals reportedly measure up to 10 cm or slightly more.

This species can have several colour morphs; the most common are blue and brown. Depending on the environment, diet and age, the colour can vary from almost transparent to shiny beige.

No data is available on the maximum lifespan in the wild. According to a study, when appropriately cared for, they lived up to 5–6 years, but the average lifespan is around 3–4 years. In captivity, life expectancy depends on factors such as disease, diet, poor living conditions and shipment stress.

Plants: Cuban crayfish cannot be kept in planted tanks. They will eat, cut and uproot just about any plant. The only viable options are plastic plants, floating plants, or cheap plants you are ready to lose and replace.

Molting: the exoskeleton limits growth, so crayfish periodically shed it. Before molting, the crayfish becomes less active, stops eating and seeks shelter; otherwise it can easily fall prey to tankmates. Never disturb a molting crayfish, and do not panic if you do not see it for a few days. Keep putting food in the tank, keep giving calcium-rich food, and do not remove the old exoskeleton, as it contains minerals and the crayfish will eat it later.

Tankmates: Cuban crayfish are aggressive and predatory, and territorial (especially males). Males are extremely likely to fight when housed together. They should not be kept in a community tank with fish, freshwater snails, small frogs, crabs and other crayfish species. Bottom-dwelling, slow-moving or long-finned fish (like Betta) will be the first to get hurt. Adult Cuban crayfish usually do not hunt dwarf shrimp, which are too small and fast, but they are opportunistic and will eat whatever they catch.

Overall, Procambarus cubensis is a simple species to care for and can be recommended even for beginners. The biggest concern is their aggression.
